subject: Animation
title: Rankin/Bass Holiday Specials
description: Learn Rankin/Bass Holiday Specials in one minute.

hook.text: Every December, millions of Americans watch Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, a 1964 stop-motion special.

buildup.text: Rankin/Bass produced dozens of holiday specials using stop-motion puppets they called Animagic.

discovery.text: The specials were animated in Japan by Tadahito Mochinaga's studio, not in the United States.

twist.text: The original Rudolph puppets were lost for decades before being found in a private attic in 2005.

climax.text: Rankin/Bass specials introduced stop-motion to millions and became permanent fixtures of American culture.

punchline.text: A misfit reindeer puppet became America's holiday tradition.

quiz.question: Where were the Rankin/Bass holiday specials actually animated?
options: In Japan, by Tadahito Mochinaga's studio

details.summary: Rankin/Bass produced beloved holiday specials like Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer (1964) using 'Animagic' stop-motion. Their specials became annual television traditions that introduced generations of Americans to puppet animation.
details.whyItMatters: Rankin/Bass specials are among the most-watched animated programs ever. They embedded stop-motion into American popular culture and created a tradition of animated holiday storytelling on television.
takeaways: Rankin/Bass created enduring holiday specials using stop-motion
Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer has aired annually since 1964
Their 'Animagic' technique introduced millions to puppet animation

faq.question: Where were the Rankin/Bass specials actually animated?
faq.answer: The animation was produced in Japan by MOM Production and later Topcraft. Rankin/Bass handled story and voice recording in the US, then shipped materials to Japan where skilled animators created the stop-motion sequences.

faq.question: Why do Rankin/Bass specials still air every year?
faq.answer: Networks pay for the rights because the specials consistently draw large audiences across generations. The nostalgic connection is so strong that families watch them as cultural rituals, making them reliable ratings performers.
